body_text: You may have noticed something about the web these days. Specifically, how pretty much every new website looks hastily vibecoded, with copy full of Claudeisms, and a nearly identical CSS framework that, in the argot of LLMs, isn’t just formulaic — it’s synthetic. Well, now you too can have this cookie-cutter aesthetic on even the most handcrafted website, with Slopstrap , a new CSS framework by Mike Lacher that can make any website appear to be hacked together in five minutes in Claude. Random words italicized for emphasis? Wherever you want. Random blinking status indicators? Loads of ‘em! The kind of rounded, shiny button that I’m sure was eye-catching at the beginning of the vibecoding boom but which now simply melts into the background because it’s literally everywhere? You betcha. A bunch of cards with pointless stats on them? Galore . Save the tokens, just make your site an uninspired 2026 cliche with one CSS package . The nature of the end has been a matter of consideration for time immemorial, from the psychedelic if symbolic visions of the revelation of John, the fantasies of atomic annihilation of the Cold War to the realities of kinetic destruction of the Cretaceous. How does the apocalypse proceed? Is it a sharp destruction, such as the Fall of Troy, or a gradual and barely imperceptible decline in state capacity, such as the Fall of Rome? I speak, of course, of the SaaSpocalypse. The foretold doom of the software business, hastened along by the rise of AI. This past and these next two weeks, we see earnings from a number of big names in the once-booming software-as-a-service industry who once feared the fiery doom of a swift AI-driven demise but have survived that; Salesforce seem like they’re going to ride this thing out. But don’t let that deceive you. Just because the margins of the SaaS companies have not been atomized by arsenals of agents doesn’t mean that a slow-moving apocalypse isn’t in motion in some areas. Indeed, it has been going on for quite some time. The name of the fourth horseman of this SaaSPocalypse is not ChatGPT Codex, though. It’s Bending Spoons , which released earnings last Thursday and announced a new acquisition that advances its mission of rolling up the detritus of the SaaS boom into a viable firm. You may not know Bending Spoons off the dome, but you know (and may very well use!) their products. The company went public over the summer and has set out to buy up companies that once had sky-high valuations but have since abruptly returned to reality. The classic format of a Bending Spoons headline is something like “[ Somewhat recognizable app ]-owner Bending Spoons purchases [ slightly more well-known app ].” You have seen this headline a dozen times. In fact, you can build a pretty reliable timeline of the company by daisy-chaining headlines in this exact format: July, 2024: Italy’s Bending Spoons Buys WeTransfer September, 2025 : WeTransfer owner Bending Spoons buys Vimeo December, 2025 : Vimeo owner Bending Spoons buys AOL July, 2026 : AOL Owner Bending Spoons jumps 40% after IPO August, 2026 : Newly public Bending Spoons buys AirTable Their modus operandi is to buy up mature companies that have maximized their total addressable market at a fraction of their once-high valuations, and then put these relatively boring businesses under the control of small, well-paid teams to manage them . Crucially, Bending Spoons employees run the apps they own, with previous staff usually let go in large-scale layoffs pretty quickly after the acquisition. And it’s not just layoffs, either. Bending Spoons relies on price hikes too. So, lower overhead, higher revenue, a decently-locked in user base, you get the ideal. Berkshire Hathaway , the investment firm that built an empire by investing in boring companies like utilities and insurance companies that had unsexy businesses that spun off cash predictably, has acquired a 10% stake in the company. Last week, they struck again, buying Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68 billion, which is a third of the price paid by Intuit in 2021. While the various AI-driven news cycles have rattled the valuations of the SaaS giants, they seem fine, right? Saaspocalypse averted? Not quite, and this week will be revealing. Just because the Saaspocalypse doesn’t look like the overnight collapse of an empire doesn’t mean it’s not happening. Lots of these companies are trading at a fraction of their valuation and an even smaller fraction of their aspirations. Heck, this week we’ll get an update from Zoom , which is trucking along at a $24.5 billion market cap, not meaningfully different from where they were trading in 2019 before the pandemic that propelled them, at one point, north of a $140 billion market valuation. They say that the standard civilian experience of the fall of the Roman empire was when your local bridge went out and nobody came around to fix it. title: 🥊 Retailers beat the bad vibes
body_text: A slew of states have now enacted cell phone bans in schools, which keep phones, watches and connected tablets locked away from bell-to-bell. Some of the immediate benefits, like encouraging students to, uhhh, talk to each other, are obvious. Harvard researchers, however, took things a step further. They looked at students in 4,600 schools across the US and found that school cell phone bans helped students learn more. They found that in schools where phones and other devices were kept locked away during the day, students gained the academic equivalent of one to two additional weeks of instruction per year, the Wall Street Journal reported . “Pretty soon we’ll look back and think it’s crazy that students could use their phones whenever they want to,” Thomas Kane, an author of the study and director of the Harvard Center for Education Policy Research, told the WSJ. Earlier this week I wrote that American consumers feeling increasingly pessimistic about the cost of living was increasingly not Walmart ’s problem. Case in point: The retail giant reported earnings results that narrowly beat Wall Street estimates and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. Its US e-commerce sales jumped 23%, even as comparable sales growth slowed from a year earlier. Target , another place that sells both staples and cheap knickknacks, crushed quarterly estimates and hiked its guidance after posting its best sales growth in five years. TJX , which owns discount retailers TJ Maxx and Marshalls, also beat estimates. These retailers describe catering to a value-conscious customer. “Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend, and we see them responding when we give them something they love at a price that feels right,” Cara Sylvester, chief merchandising officer at Target, told analysts. US retail sales slowed in October as purchases of big-ticket items like cars and furniture slipped, according to the most recent reading from the Commerce Department released Tuesday. That checks out with what both Home Depot and Lowe’s reported: smaller repair and maintenance projects helped drive their sales beats, even as larger discretionary renovations remained under pressure. Both face macroeconomic headwinds, like high borrowing costs and a slow housing market. “Well, Simeon, housing turnover hasn't moved in four years now,” Richard McPhail, Home Depot’s current CFO and incoming CEO, quipped at a Morgan Stanley analyst. He attributed several positive quarters to market share gains. “Our investments are designed to position us to capture share regardless of the economic environment,” he said. Retailers seem to be successfully adapting to a world where people are pinching pennies and feel like life is ripping them off. Target is cutting prices, TJ Maxx is trying to attract bargain hunters across income brackets, and Home Depot is catering to homeowners who would rather fix up their current place than trade their cheap mortgage for a much more expensive one. The industry appears to be well poised for a strong holiday shopping season. For now, retailers seem to have figured out how to keep Americans spending even when they don't feel particularly good about it. The question is how long that can last if the cost of living keeps squeezing their budgets. 🏈 NFL: This Sunday sees a big game between the two teams atop the NFC, with the Vikings taking on the 49ers. title: 👍 Nvidia will probably be fine
body_text: Americans are in love with fried chicken, but that fervor has largely sidestepped KFC. The Yum Brands chain’s US sales keep falling and the pain is hitting franchises: a major franchisee is filing for bankruptcy, according to court filings . Tasty Chick’n LLC operates 75 KFCs and 9 Taco Bells across 10 Southeastern and Midwestern states and owes Yum more than $15 million in unpaid royalties. (Franchisees operate as independent businesses but must pay portions of their sales to the franchisor.) Franchise agreements can require remodelling and other upgrades to locations and that appears to be the root of the unpaid royalties in this case – another reminder that when big, national fast food chains embark on turnarounds, there’s often a bevy of regional operators footing most of the bill. In one of the most anticipated quarterly earnings reports in years, on Tuesday Nvidia bested Wall Street’s expectations for earnings and revenue and posted guidance ahead of analysts’ estimates. So that means the Jensen Huang saga is firmly behind the chip behemoth, right? Right? Insert Padme meme here . A bevy of Silicon Valley bigwigs are now calling for Huang’s reinstatement. Nevermind the looming Capital Hill hearings , the only-just-begun internal corporate investigations into who knew what, and whatever the federal law enforcement agencies and securities regulators might choose to do, Elon Musk and a bevy of venture capitalists think Huang and only Huang can be an effective CEO of Nvidia. For his part, Huang has been listening, learning, and reflecting. And, in a statement released five days after he tendered his resignation, he’s decided that he’s open to returning as CEO of the company he co-founded. (The board says it has ruled out his return and has reached out to Arm Holdings Plc Chief Executive Officer Rene Haas, Bloomberg News reported Wednesday.) The stock has taken a beating in recent months. As Entrypoint’s Luke Kawa pointed out, the company is paradoxically in an extremely strong position , and investors could stand to benefit thanks to both the (relatively) beaten down shares and the continued demand for AI chips. “Demand did not resign,” was the quip from Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. In Kawa’s estimation, interim CEO Colette Kress “her hands are on the wheel of a profit powerhouse that’s on cruise control thanks to the prior navigator.” They say one sign of an effective manager is if the organization they run can operate effectively without them. It’s understandable that many executives would rather not find out if they’ve achieved that kind of success, but Huang very well may have. The road back – at least, at Nvidia – looks very much like a dead-end at the moment. Things might be different if Nvidia’s biggest customers were jumping ship. But they’re not really doing that. Amazon ’s Jeff Bezos declined to say whether Huang should be reinstated, saying he lacked enough information to voice an opinion. OpenAI’s Sam Altman – who knows a bit about being ousted and reinstated at the helm of an organization he helped create – expressed “extreme, extreme gratitude” for Huang taking an early bet on OpenAI, and said it’s “hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.” But as Huang surely recognizes, that’s not exactly a clarion call for his return. That’s particularly indicative of the slim chances Huang has for a reinstatement, given Altman is arguably the AI exec most plugged into the network of Bay Area venture capitalists who have been most strident in their support for the ex-Nvidia CEO’s return.
